hints: Separate the variables so that all $y$-terms are with $dy$ and all $x$-terms are with $dx$.
Integrate $\dfrac1y$ and use the substitution $u=1+x^2$ for $\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$.
Use $x=0$, $y=2$ to determine the integration constant before exponentiating.
Since $1+x^2>0$ and the initial value is positive, choose the positive square-root form and simplify.
walkthrough:
Separate variables in the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{xy}{1+x^2}$ by dividing by $y$ and multiplying by $\mathrm{d}x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{y}\,\mathrm{d}y = \dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Evaluate the right-hand integral by recognizing the derivative of the denominator, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(1+x^2) = 2x$:
$$\int \dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2} \int \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2)$$

Combine into the general implicit equation with an integration constant $C$:
$$\ln|y| = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C$$

Apply the initial condition $y = 2$ when $x = 0$ to find the constant $C$:
$$\ln(2) = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+0^2) + C = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1) + C$$
Since $\ln(1) = 0$:
$$C = \ln 2$$

Substitute $C = \ln 2$ back into the solution (noting that $y > 0$ so $|y| = y$):
$$\ln y = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + \ln 2$$

Use logarithm laws to combine the terms on the right side:
$$\ln y = \ln\left[(1+x^2)^{1/2}\right] + \ln 2 = \ln\left[2(1+x^2)^{1/2}\right]$$

Exponentiate both sides to obtain the explicit simplified expression for $y$:
$$y = 2\sqrt{1+x^2}$$

ai_rubric.Solving Separable Differential Equations: Separates variables, $\int \dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx=\int\dfrac1y\,dy$. Derives the term $\ln y$. The final result is $y=2\sqrt{1+x^2}$.
